title: The last province, and the crown
summary: Close the pre-algebra map with counting and probability: count the opposite, count every pair, and work out the chance of a small thing. Then take the arc's hardest proof, that no fraction will ever square to 2, and spend it on a length you can draw.
materials: the field journal, open at the sprint's proof pages
a compass and a ruler for the diagonal and the number line
two ordinary dice and a handful of socks or counters in two colours
the twelve coins and the balance, out on the table for the monster

problems.prompt: A song is in four four, which means four beats to a bar. The chorus starts on the first beat of bar 17. If the very first beat of the song is beat 1, which beat number is that?
explanation: Bars come in equal blocks, so count the blocks that finish before the one you want.
Sixteen whole bars go past before bar 17 begins, and sixteen bars of four beats is 64 beats.
The next beat is the one the chorus starts on, which is beat 65 itself. Answering 64 counts the beats that finished.
problems.useAgain: when things arrive in equal blocks and you need the number of the first one in a later block.
hints: Sixteen whole bars go by before bar 17 starts. Count those before you count anything else.
Multiply the bars that have already finished by the beats in a bar, then take one more step.
problems.socraticHint: If the song had numbered its first beat as beat 0, which beat would bar 17 begin on?

variant.prompt: The song is in three four, three beats to a bar, and the verse starts on the first beat of bar 21. Which beat number is that?

problems.prompt: A drummer plays a warm-up ladder. In section 1 he plays one hit on every beat. Each new section doubles the hits that land on a beat. How many hits land on one beat in section 6?
explanation: Section 1 is where the ladder starts, so no doubling has happened yet.
From section 1 to section 6 there are five doublings, not six, which is 2 multiplied by itself five times.
Writing the row out is the safe way: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Doubling six times and landing on 64 is the trap.
problems.useAgain: when a number doubles or triples the same way over and over and you need a later step.
hints: Section 1 is one hit, not two. Write the sections out in a row before you jump ahead.
Count the doublings that actually happen between section 1 and section 6, then apply that many.
problems.socraticHint: How many doublings sit between section 1 and section 6, and is that the same number as six?

variant.prompt: Section 1 is again one hit a beat, but now each section triples the hits on a beat. How many hits land on one beat in section 4?

problems.prompt: A section is 48 bars long and every bar has 3 beats. The band plays it at 90 beats a minute. How long does the section last?
explanation: Beats first, clock second. Forty-eight bars of three beats is 144 beats.
Ninety beats a minute is a per, and it turns into one and a half beats every second.
So 144 beats take 144 divided by 1.5, which is 96 seconds, or 1 minute 36 seconds. Reading 144 beats as 144 seconds gives 2 minutes 24 and is the trap.
problems.useAgain: when a speed is given as a per and you need to turn an amount into a time.
hints: Beats are not seconds. Work out how many beats the section holds before you go near the clock.
Turn 90 beats a minute into beats each second, then divide the beats by that.
problems.socraticHint: How many beats go past in one single second at this tempo?

variant.prompt: A section is 32 bars long with 4 beats in every bar, played at 160 beats a minute. How long does it last?

problem.prompt: Nine dots sit in a three by three square grid, evenly spaced, three rows of three. How many squares can you make using four of the dots as corners? Count every square, including any that sits at an angle.
explanation: Search in an order, because a hunt with no order always misses one.
Flat squares with a side of one step: four of them, one in each corner of the grid.
Flat squares with a side of two steps: one, the big one round the outside. That is five, and five is where most people stop.
Now the one that hides. Join the four dots in the middle of the four edges and you get a square standing on its corner.
Four and one and one is six. A square does not stop being a square when you turn it.
problem.useAgain: when you are counting shapes inside a picture and want to be sure none were missed.
hints: Five of them are easy to find. The sixth is not sitting flat.
Group your search first: by side length, and then by whether the square is flat or tilted.
problem.socraticHint: Does a square stop being a square when you turn it halfway between two corners?

variant.prompt: Sixteen dots sit in a four by four square grid, evenly spaced. How many squares can you make using four of the dots as corners, tilted ones included?

steps.title: The last province: counting the opposite, every pair, and the chance of a small thing

problems.prompt: A three digit code is made from the digits 1 to 5, and digits are allowed to repeat. How many of those codes use at least one 5?
explanation: Three slots with five choices in each gives 5 times 5 times 5, which is 125 codes.
At least one 5 is awkward head on, because those codes come in three overlapping piles.
The opposite is one clean job: a code with no 5 has four choices per slot, which is 64.
So the answer is 125 take away 64, which is 61.
problems.useAgain: when a question says at least one and the opposite of it can be said in a single sentence.
hints: Counting the codes with one 5, then two 5s, then three 5s is three jobs and an easy place to count something twice.
Count all the codes there are, then count the ones with no 5 at all, and take one from the other.
problems.socraticHint: Which is easier to describe in one sentence: a code that has a 5 somewhere, or a code that has no 5 anywhere?

variant.prompt: A four digit code is made from the digits 1 to 3, and digits may repeat. How many of those codes use at least one 3?

problems.prompt:
Marcus counted the diagonals of a nine-sided shape like this:
Line 1: Every diagonal joins a pair of corners, so start by counting every pair of the nine corners: 9 times 8, which is 72.
Line 2: That count treats each pair as two different orderings, once from each corner's point of view, so it counts every line twice.
Line 3: 72 lines counted twice means there are really 72 different lines between corners.
Line 4: A nine-sided shape has nine sides, so take those away: 72 minus 9 leaves 63 diagonals.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 3 is wrong: catching the double count is only half the job. 72 counted twice really means 36 different lines, not 72.
Lines 1 and 2 are both correct: 9 times 8 really is 72, and that counts every line from both of its ends.
Line 4 correctly takes away the nine sides. It just takes them away from the wrong total.
Halving 72 gives 36 lines in total, and taking away the nine sides leaves 27 diagonals, not 63.
problems.useAgain: when you count something in pairs and catch that you have double counted, but still have to act on what you caught.
hints: Noticing the double count and fixing it are two separate steps. Check that both of them actually happened.
A total counted from both ends needs an actual division by two, not just a sentence about it.
problems.socraticHint: If nine friends each named every pair they were in, would every pair get named once or twice?

variant.prompt:
Priya counted the handshakes at a gathering of 12 people like this:
Line 1: Every person can shake hands with anyone at the gathering, so start with 12 times 12, which is 144.
Line 2: That count is already exactly every handshake counted twice, so dividing it by 2 will give the right answer.
Line 3: Divide 144 by 2: 72.
Line 4: So there are 72 handshakes at the gathering.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: A flat ten sided shape has a straight line drawn between every pair of its corners. Some of those lines are the sides of the shape itself. How many of them are diagonals?
explanation: Every line joins one pair of corners, so count pairs: 10 times 9 halved, which is 45 lines.
That 45 counts the sides too, because a side also joins a pair of corners.
A ten sided shape has ten sides, so 45 take away 10 leaves 35 diagonals.
The trap is forgetting to halve, or forgetting the sides were caught in the same net.
problems.useAgain: when a count of pairs includes some pairs you did not want, and it is easier to remove them than to avoid them.
hints: Count every line between every pair of corners first, and do not worry yet about which ones are sides.
Once you have all the lines, work out how many of them are sides and take those out.
problems.socraticHint: Is a side of the shape also a line between two corners?

variant.prompt: A flat twelve sided shape has a straight line drawn between every pair of its corners. How many of those lines are diagonals?

problems.prompt: You roll two ordinary dice. What is the chance the two numbers add up to 10?
explanation: Imagine one die red and the other blue. Six faces each gives 36 rolls, all equally likely.
Three of them add to ten: four and six, five and five, six and four.
Three out of 36 is one twelfth. Treating four and six as one roll loses a case.
problems.useAgain: when every outcome is equally likely and you can count the ones you want against the ones there are.
hints: The two dice are different dice. A four on one and a six on the other is not the same roll as a six on one and a four on the other.
Write out every pair that adds to ten, then say how many rolls there are altogether.
problems.socraticHint: How many rolls are there in total if you imagine one die painted red and the other painted blue?

variant.prompt: You roll two ordinary dice. What is the chance the two numbers add up to 5?

problems.prompt: You roll an ordinary die twice. What is the chance you get at least one six? Give the answer as a fraction.
explanation: At least one six covers three overlapping stories, and adding them up double counts the pair of sixes.
The opposite is one clean story: no six at all, which needs a not-six twice.
Five sixths times five sixths is 25 out of 36.
So the chance of at least one six is one whole take away that, which is 11 over 36.
problems.useAgain: when at least one appears in a chance question and the no-such-thing case is one clean story.
hints: At least one six hides three different stories, and the easiest one to forget is both dice showing six.
Work out the chance of no six at all first, then take that away from one whole.
problems.socraticHint: What is the only way to roll a die twice and not get at least one six?

variant.prompt: You roll an ordinary die twice. What is the chance you get at least one number bigger than 4? Give the answer as a fraction.

problems.prompt: A drawer holds 5 red socks and 3 blue socks. You pull out two socks without looking. What is the chance both of them are red? Give the answer as a fraction.
explanation: Count pairs rather than socks. Eight socks make 8 times 7 halved, which is 28 pairs, all equally likely.
Pairs that are two reds: 5 times 4 halved, which is 10.
Ten out of 28 tidies to 5 over 14.
Multiplying five eighths by five eighths pretends nothing left the drawer, and that is the trap.
problems.useAgain: when things are taken out and not put back, so the pile changes between one pick and the next.
hints: The second sock does not come out of the same drawer the first one did, because a sock has already left.
Count how many pairs of socks exist altogether, then how many of those pairs are two reds.
problems.socraticHint: How many different pairs of socks could you have ended up holding?

variant.prompt: A jar holds 4 green marbles and 5 yellow marbles. You take two out without looking. What is the chance both are green? Give the answer as a fraction.

problems.prompt: A four beat bar is filled by choosing, for each beat on its own, either a drum or a clap. How many different bars use at least one clap?
explanation: Every beat is its own choice with two answers. Four beats give 2 times 2 times 2 times 2, which is 16 bars.
Only one of the 16 has no clap: the bar that is drums all the way through.
Take it out and 15 are left. Answering 16 forgets that one bar has to go.
problems.useAgain: when each step of a thing is chosen separately and you want how many whole things are possible.
hints: Each beat is a separate choice with two answers, so count every bar there is before you worry about claps.
How many of those bars have no clap in them at all?
problems.socraticHint: How many bars would there be if the bar had one beat, and then two? What does the count do each time a beat is added?

variant.prompt: A five beat bar is filled by choosing, for each beat, either a drum or a clap. How many different bars use at least one drum?

steps.title: A different container measured, and which trial got closer

problems.prompt: A small tank is 10 cm long, 6 cm wide and 5 cm tall. What is its volume, in cubic cm?
explanation: Multiply all three edges: 10 times 6 times 5.
10 times 6 is 60, and 60 times 5 is 300 cubic cm.
problems.useAgain: when a different container's volume is needed, using the same multiply-all-three-edges rule.
hints: Multiply the length and width first, then multiply by the height.
Keep the final unit cubic, since three lengths were multiplied.
problems.socraticHint: Does the order you multiply the three edges in change the final volume?

variant.prompt: A small tank is 12 cm long, 4 cm wide and 5 cm tall. What is its volume, in cubic cm?

problems.prompt: That same 10 cm by 6 cm by 5 cm tank has 6 faces. What is its total surface area, in square cm?
explanation: The three face areas are 10 by 6, 10 by 5 and 6 by 5, which are 60, 50 and 30.
60 plus 50 plus 30 is 140, then doubled for the matching pair of each face.
140 times 2 is 280 square cm.
problems.useAgain: when a container's surface area is found from its three pairs of faces, keeping the unit flat, not cubic.
hints: Find each of the three different face areas separately.
Add them, then double the total.
problems.socraticHint: If the volume answer came out in cubic cm, should the surface area answer share that same kind of unit?

variant.prompt: That same 12 cm by 4 cm by 5 cm tank's surface area, in square cm?

problems.prompt: A fair die is rolled 50 times and a 6 comes up 9 times. What fraction of the 50 rolls, in lowest terms, showed a 6?
explanation: The simulated fraction is 9 over 50.
9/50 is already in lowest terms, since 9 and 50 share no common factor.
This is closer to the calculated 1/6 (about 0.17) than a shorter run tends to land.
problems.useAgain: when a bigger simulation run is compared to the same calculated chance as a smaller one, to see if it lands closer.
hints: Write the tally count over the total rolls.
Check whether the fraction simplifies further.
problems.socraticHint: Does rolling more times tend to bring the simulated fraction closer to the calculated chance, or further from it?

variant.prompt: A fair die is rolled 50 times and a 6 comes up 7 times. What fraction of the 50 rolls, in lowest terms, showed a 6?

problems.prompt: In 20 rolls, a 6 showed up 1/4 of the time. In 50 rolls, a 6 showed up 9/50 of the time. The true chance is 1/6, about 0.17. Which fraction landed closer to it?
explanation: 1/4 is 0.25, which is 0.08 away from the true 0.17.
9/50 is 0.18, which is only 0.01 away from 0.17.
The longer run of 50 rolls landed closer to the true, calculated chance, as longer runs tend to do.
problems.useAgain: when comparing two simulation runs of different lengths to see which one wobbled closer to the true, calculated chance.
hints: Turn both fractions into decimals so they are easy to compare.
Find how far each decimal sits from the true 0.17, then compare those two gaps.
problems.socraticHint: Between a short run and a longer run, which one usually wobbles further from the true, calculated chance?

variant.prompt: In 20 rolls, a 6 showed up 1/5 of the time. In 50 rolls, a 6 showed up 6/50 of the time. The true chance is 1/6, about 0.17. Which fraction landed closer to it?

figure.alt: White to move. A white knight on e4 faces the black king on g8 and a black queen on d7.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move checks the king and attacks the queen at the same time?
explanation: A knight landing on f6 checks the king on g8 and attacks the queen on d7 in the same move.
Black must answer the check first, so the queen cannot escape in time.
White wins the queen next move, the biggest fork on the board.
problems.useAgain: when a single knight move checks the king and threatens the queen together.
hints: Look for a knight move that touches the black king's own square.
Check whether that same square also touches the black queen.
problems.socraticHint: If black must answer check first, does the queen get a turn to run?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move checks the king and attacks the queen at the same time?

figure.alt: White to move. A white knight on d5 faces the black king on a8 and a black queen on d7.
White to move. A white queen on h2 faces the black king on f6 with a black rook on b6 behind it on the same rank.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move forces the king to move and wins the rook behind it?
explanation: Black's king on f6 and rook on b6 share the same rank.
Qh6 checks the king first, so it must step off that rank.
Once the king moves, the rook behind it is exposed on the same line.
problems.useAgain: when a check lines up with a bigger prize sitting further along the same rank.
hints: Which rank already holds both the black king and the black rook?
Move your queen onto that rank so it checks the king first.
problems.socraticHint: After the king moves out of check, what is still sitting on that rank?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move forces the king to move and wins the rook behind it?

figure.alt: White to move. A white queen on b5 faces the black king on c3 with a black rook on g7 behind it on the same diagonal.
White to move. Black's lone king sits on h8, white's bishop on h6 and queen on g1.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?
explanation: Your bishop on h6 already guards the square g7 next to the black king.
Qg7 checks the king and cannot be captured, because the bishop defends it.
The king has no square left to run to, so it is mate.
problems.useAgain: when a piece defends the exact square your queen needs to deliver mate on.
hints: Which square next to the black king does your bishop already guard?
Move your queen onto that same protected square.
problems.socraticHint: What piece is standing behind the queen, ready to recapture?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?

figure.alt: White to move. Black's lone king sits on a8, white's bishop on a6 and queen on b1.
Black to move. Black's king sits alone on h8, with a white king on f7 and a white pawn on g6.

problems.prompt: It is black's move. The king has no square to go to and looks trapped. Is this checkmate, stalemate, or does black have another legal move?
explanation: Black's king on h8 cannot move to g8 or g7, both covered by the white king, and h7 is covered by the pawn.
But nothing white actually attacks h8 itself right now.
No legal move and no check together mean stalemate, even though the king looks completely trapped.
problems.useAgain: when a king looks completely trapped, so always check whether it is actually in check before calling it mate.
hints: List every square next to the king and who covers each one.
Now check the king's own square. Is anything actually attacking it?
problems.socraticHint: Does a king with no moves always mean the game is over by checkmate?

variant.prompt: It is black's move. The king has no square to go to and looks trapped. Is this checkmate, stalemate, or does black have another legal move?

figure.alt: Black to move. Black's king sits alone on a8, with a white king on b6 and a white pawn on c7.

steps.title: The promise from week 5, and how a crown gets taken
steps.body:
Week 5 left you a promise and did not keep it. It said, out loud, that there are lengths sitting on the number line that no fraction will ever name, and then it went off to do square roots and left the promise standing there. Today you keep it, and you keep it yourself.

Three things about how this hour runs.

Nobody is going to walk you through the argument. This is the hardest proof of the whole arc and it is yours. You have every tool it needs and you have had them for a while: supposing the opposite and watching it fall over, which is season 3's move; lowest terms and what even and odd do to a square, which you have owned since season 1; and last week's arrest, the smallest criminal, which says that if any counterexample exists at all then a smallest one exists, and a smallest one that turns out to have a smaller accomplice is a contradiction that wipes out the whole crime.

Three proofs today and no peaks, on purpose. This is a maintenance week and the proof is the heavy thing in it, so nothing is stacked beside it. Take your time. Nothing here is raced and nothing here is scored.

Write to the rubric. Every step gets a reason beside it. A proof is not the answer with some sentences round it; it is a road somebody else can walk without you standing there pointing. The test of whether you have written one is simple and it is not comfortable: hand it to somebody who does not already agree and watch where they stop.

One warning about the second problem, which is the interesting one. An argument that works is not the same as an argument that looks like it works. The season's own idea, the mirage, is about programs that run and are still wrong, and the same thing happens to proofs. When you push an argument onto a new case it will keep its shape and its confident voice whether or not it is still true. Your job is to find the exact sentence where it stops being true, and the only way to find that sentence is to write the whole thing out rather than to feel your way through it.

steps.title: The crown, and two proofs beside it

problems.prompt: The crown. Prove that no fraction squares to 2, so that root 2 is a number no fraction can ever name. Use last week's arrest: suppose some fraction does square to 2, and then take the one with the smallest bottom number there could possibly be. Show that one has an accomplice smaller than itself. Write the whole argument out with a reason beside every step, and finish by saying in one sentence what the contradiction has proved.

mustMention: suppose a fraction squares to 2 and take the one with the smallest bottom number
squaring gives a times a equals two times b times b, so a times a is even and so a is even
writing a as two times c forces b times b to be even as well, so b is even too
both being even makes a smaller fraction that also squares to 2, which the smallest one cannot have

explanation: Suppose the opposite, which is season 3's move: suppose some fraction squares to 2.
If even one exists, one of them has the smallest bottom there is, and arresting that one is the plan.
Call it a over b. Squaring gives a times a equals 2 times b times b, so a times a is even.
An odd number times itself is odd, so a is even and can be written as 2 times c.
Substituting shows b times b equals 2 times c times c, so b is even too.
Halve both to get a fraction that still squares to 2 with a smaller bottom. The smallest had a smaller one, so it never existed.
problems.useAgain: when a claim says no number of a certain shape can do a job, and you want to prove it instead of testing examples forever.
hints: Do not go hunting for the fraction. Suppose it exists, and then look at the smallest one there could be.
Square both sides first, then ask what the equation forces about whether the top number is odd or even.
problems.socraticHint: If a and b both turn out to be even, is a over b still the fraction with the smallest bottom number?

problems.prompt: Now stress the argument you just wrote. First run the same arrest on root 3: suppose a fraction squares to 3, take the one with the smallest bottom number, and produce a smaller accomplice. Then try to run the same arrest on root 4, which is 2 and is obviously a fraction. Write both attempts out in full, then name the exact sentence where the root 4 attempt dies, and say why that sentence was fine the first time and is not fine now.

mustMention: for root 3, a times a is a multiple of three, and because three is prime a itself is a multiple of three
the same steps then make b a multiple of three and give a fraction with a smaller bottom
the root 4 attempt dies at the step from a times a being a multiple of four to a being a multiple of four
two squared is four, so a square can be a multiple of four while the number itself is not

explanation: Root 3 first. Suppose a over b squares to 3 with the smallest bottom, so a times a equals 3 times b times b.
Three is prime, and a prime dividing a product divides one of its parts. Both parts are a, so a is 3 times c.
Substituting gives b times b equals 3 times c times c, so b is a multiple of three too, and the bottom shrinks.
Now root 4, whose opening is word for word the same.
The next sentence is where it dies. Four is not prime, and 2 squared is 4, so a square can be a multiple of four while the number is not.
Nothing forces a to be 4 times c, so no accomplice appears. Both attempts had the same shape; only one had a true sentence there.
problems.useAgain: when an argument worked once and you want to know whether it really works for the next case or only looks as though it would.
hints: The two attempts differ in exactly one sentence. Write both of them out fully before you go hunting for it.
Ask what three being prime buys you in the first attempt, and then check whether four buys you the same thing.
problems.socraticHint: Is there a whole number whose square is a multiple of four but which is not itself a multiple of four?

problems.prompt: Last, spend the crown on something you can see. Draw a square with sides one unit long and draw one diagonal across it. Use week 6's theorem to say exactly how long that diagonal is. Then swing the diagonal down flat onto a number line with a compass and mark where it lands. Write down what you have just built, in one sentence. Then answer the objection a calculator makes, which is that the length is 1.4142135.

mustMention: the diagonal is the long side of a right triangle whose two short sides are both one
so the diagonal squared is two and the diagonal is exactly root 2
swinging it onto the number line marks a real point that no fraction names
1.4142135 is itself a fraction and its square is not exactly two, so it is a near neighbour and not the number

explanation: Cut the square along its diagonal and you hold a right triangle whose two short sides are both one.
The cut-and-rearrange theorem says one squared plus one squared equals the long side squared.
So the diagonal squared is two, and the diagonal is exactly root 2.
That length is not an idea, it is on your paper. A compass swings it onto the number line and marks a point.
The crown says no fraction ever names that point, so the line has points the fractions miss. That is week 5's promise, kept.
About the calculator: that decimal is itself a fraction, and squaring it lands just under two. Looking right is not being right.
problems.useAgain: when you want to show that something you can draw is not something you can write as a fraction.
hints: The diagonal is not a new mystery. It is the long side of a right triangle whose short sides you already know.
Once you know exactly what the length is, ask what the crown said about that particular number.
problems.socraticHint: If you multiplied 1.4142135 by itself by hand, would you land on 2, or on something just underneath it?

steps.title: The twelve coins, still on the card
steps.body:
The monster stays where it is. It went on the home card last week and it comes off it when you say so, and not before.

The story again, unchanged: twelve coins that look identical. Eleven weigh the same. One is a fake and it is either heavier or lighter, and nobody tells you which. You have a balance with two pans and no numbers on it, and you may use it three times. Find the fake, and say whether it is heavy or light.

Nobody is teaching this today and nothing here is a hint about how to weigh. Three things instead, all of them bookkeeping.

Keep a proper page for it in the journal. Every weighing you try, what the pans did, and what that ruled out. Casework is a thing you have owned since last season, and this is the biggest piece of casework anybody has handed you. A plan that lives only in your head will collapse the third time you pick the coins up.

Use the real coins and the real balance. Twelve identical coins in your hands behave differently from twelve coins in your imagination, and the pan tips before you have finished thinking, which is the whole pleasure of it.

And one question worth sitting with this week, which is a counting question and not a weighing one, and it happens to be the exact kind of counting the skills lane spent this morning on. Before you weigh anything at all, how many different endings does this puzzle have? Not how many coins. How many complete answers of the form which coin it is and which kind of wrong it is. Count them and write the number in the journal. You are not being asked to do anything with that number yet.

The coins have the rest of this week and all of next. Nobody is asking you for them today.

steps.title: Why counting the opposite is allowed
steps.prompt: Write a page for somebody who has never seen this move, and who is suspicious of it because it looks like cheating. Say what counting the opposite is. Then say why it is legal, which comes down to one sentence you have to be able to say out loud: every single case sits in exactly one of the two piles, so nothing is lost and nothing is counted twice. Use two of this morning's problems as your worked examples, one about counting and one about chance. Then, and this is the part that shows you understand it, give one example where counting the opposite would be the worse road, and say what makes it worse there.

steps.title: Say the crown out loud
steps.prompt: Two minutes, standing, no paper and no notes. Tell the root 2 proof to somebody who has not seen it. Start with what you are trying to show, say what you suppose and why supposing it is allowed, walk the steps with a reason on each one, and land on why the contradiction settles the matter for every fraction there will ever be. Then answer one question they ask you about it, and if the question is one you cannot answer, say so out loud rather than covering it.
